EvoPrune instead merges tokens at selected encoder layers after standard multi-head self-attention, ranking candidate token pairs with a composite score matrix that combines semantic similarity (merging redundant tokens), information diversity (discouraging merging of distinct content), and attention-based importance (preserving reasoning-critical tokens); the highest-scoring pairs are merged and propagated onward in a hierarchical, progressive fashion [S2][S3].

value.question: How do BLIP-2's Q-Former and Chain-of-Sight's visual resamplers each use learnable queries?
value.answer: In BLIP-2, the Q-Former takes a set number of learnable query embeddings as input to its image transformer; these queries interact with one another (and optionally with text) through self-attention layers and with the frozen image features through cross-attention layers inserted every other block, yielding a fixed number of output features independent of input image resolution [S1]. These queries act as an information bottleneck that extracts the visual features most useful for the frozen LLM [S3], and at VQA fine-tuning time question tokens can be fed in to interact with the queries via self-attention so the cross-attention focuses on informative regions [S4]. In Chain-of-Sight, learnable queries are instead allocated per window at each scale level: each windowed feature gets Ni learnable queries that cross-attend only to their corresponding window, producing N = \sum_i L^2/W_i^2 * Ni tokens; queries within the same scale share resampler parameters, while different scales use distinct parameter sets [S5].

value.question: How do Qwen-VL and CogVLM handle positional information for image features?
value.answer: For Qwen-VL, the position-aware vision-language adapter compresses visual features to a fixed length of 256 via a single-layer cross-attention module, and 2D absolute positional encodings are incorporated into the cross-attention's query-key pairs to mitigate the loss of positional detail during compression [S1]; positional information is also handled at the input/output level by encoding bounding boxes as normalized coordinate strings (range [0,1000)) tokenized as text with <box>/</box> and <ref>/</ref> special tokens, avoiding an extra positional vocabulary [S3]. The sources do not describe how CogVLM handles positional information  an it is only mentioned as following the LLaVA-style MLP projector architecture [S5].

value.question: vLLM and QLoRA both borrow paging ideas. What memory does each page?
value.answer: vLLM applies OS-style virtual memory and paging to the key-value cache: PagedAttention stores KV cache in non-contiguous fixed-size KV blocks, and a block manager maps each request's logical KV blocks to physical blocks in GPU DRAM (with CPU RAM blocks used for swapping), achieving near-zero KV cache waste [S1][S3][S4]. QLoRA instead uses "paged optimizers," i.e., paging applied to optimizer memory, to manage memory spikes during 4-bit finetuning [S5]. The QLoRA source gives only this abstract-level description, so it does not detail the mechanism or which devices the optimizer pages move between.

value.question: How do ToDRE and HoloV each avoid keeping many near-duplicate visual tokens?
value.answer: The sources only partly cover this. For HoloV, the stated remedy is to avoid attention-score-only selection, which tends to retain similar clusters of adjacent tokens with comparable attention in flat or repetitive regions [S3]; instead HoloV compresses tokens so as to preserve the image's holistic context and semantic completeness, removing redundant tokens before the LLM decoder [S2], and visualizations show it retains contextual tokens with rich semantics and key text-aligned regions even at high pruning rates (e.g., 87.5%), whereas FastV's retained set contains much redundancy [S1][S3]. For ToDRE, the provided material reports only benchmarking results of its two-stage pruning (e.g., pruning 75% of visual tokens in Stage 1 and removing the rest in Stage 2) and its title mentions token diversity and task relevance [S5]; the sources do not describe the actual mechanism by which it suppresses near-duplicate tokens.

value.question: HERO and ParVTS both use [CLS] attention from the vision encoder. What does each use it for?
value.answer: ParVTS uses attention to the [CLS] token in the vision encoder as a lightweight, supervision-free way to separate subject tokens from non-subject tokens, i.e., to group/select visual information without training [S1]. HERO instead exploits the observation that CLS attention in CLIP-ViTs follows a two-stage pattern across layers, where each stage attends to different patches encoding different granularities; it uses this to perform function-aware token selection, retaining the top tokens in each tile/thumbnail by informativeness so that complementary local-detail and global-context tokens are kept [S4][S5][S2]. The sources do not give further implementation details of how the CLS attention scores are computed in either method.

value.question: What do RedVTP and the dMLLM redundancy study each say about pruning visual tokens at the very start of diffusion VLM inference?
value.answer: The two works reach different conclusions. RedVTP argues that because visual token importance estimated from masked response tokens' attention stays consistent across steps, the less important visual tokens can be pruned right after the first inference step, maximizing efficiency and yielding large throughput/latency gains on LLaDA-V and LaViDa without hurting (and sometimes improving) accuracy [S4]. The dMLLM redundancy study, in contrast, applies pruning to the initial denoising steps and observes substantial performance drops in both from-scratch and AR-to-diffusion backbones, concluding that visual tokens play an essential role at the initial denoising stage [S2]; it instead recommends progressive or late-step pruning for from-scratch dMLLMs and layer-skipping for AR-to-diffusion models [S3]. The sources do not explain the reason for this discrepancy (e.g., differing pruning criteria or evaluation settings).

value.question: What guides pruning in Efficient3D compared with Geo3DPruner?
value.answer: The provided sources describe only Geo3DPruner (geometry-guided pruning using cross-frame geometry-aware attention with intra-voxel view-consistency and inter-voxel spatial-diversity stages) and its baselines FastV and VisPruner; they contain no information about a method called "Efficient3D," so I cannot compare what guides its pruning.

value.question: How do the SAM-based Semantic Visual Projector and AdaptVision each make the number of visual tokens depend on the image?
value.answer: For the SAM-based Semantic Visual Projector (SVP), the token count is determined by the semantic superpixels extracted from the image: SAM is prompted with a grid of points and the resulting masks are filtered to prioritize larger "whole" masks while discarding overlapping subordinate masks, decomposing an image into roughly 40 non-redundant fundamental visual elements that are each compressed and projected into visual tokens [S3]. Because common objects are often covered in one shot by whole masks while rarer scenes require subordinate (part/sub-part) masks, the number of tokens adapts to scene complexity rather than relying on a preset downsampling rate as patch-wise compressive projectors do [S1][S3][S5]. The provided sources contain no information about AdaptVision, so I cannot describe how it makes token count image-dependent.

value.question: Where in the model do InternVL-X's LVTC and LaCo compress visual tokens?
value.answer: For LVTC, compression happens inside the LLM: unlike methods that prune progressively layer by layer, LVTC compresses the visual tokens right at the input layer (via an LR projector, reducing F_V by a factor of M1²) and then expands them back at a specific layer k through Upsample2D and residual connections in the deeper layers, so most computation runs on the smaller token set [S5][S2]. The sources do not mention a method called LaCo, so its compression location cannot be answered from them.

value.question: Which operators do Skip-Vision and the operator-level visual skipping framework skip for visual tokens?
value.answer: The sources describe only the operator-level framework: it decomposes each Transformer layer into attention and FFN operators and selectively bypasses redundant attention, FFN, or both for visual tokens, while preserving the full visual-token sequence [S1][S4]. The provided sources do not mention Skip-Vision or which operators it skips, so I cannot answer that part.

value.question: Why does GPTQ quantize weights to 3-4 bits, and why does QLoRA quantize to 4 bits?
value.answer: GPTQ quantizes to 3o4 bits as a post-training compression method: it aims to compress models with hundreds of billions of parameters without significant accuracy loss, which lets the compressed OPT-175B run on a single NVIDIA A100 (or two A6000s) and gives ~3.25u00d7to-4.5u00d7 speedups from faster memory loading, whereas prior post-training methods stayed accurate only at 8 bits [S2]. QLoRA instead uses 4-bit as a low-precision *storage* data type (4-bit NormalFloat) for finetuning, dequantizing each weight tensor to BFloat16 for the matrix multiplication, so that memory is reduced enough to make finetuning large models on a single machine feasible; Double Quantization and Paged Optimizers further cut memory and prevent out-of-memory spikes [S1]. Note that 4-bit NormalFloat is motivated as information-theoretically optimal for the roughly zero-centered normal distribution of pretrained weights [S1]; the sources do not directly compare the two methods' bit-width choices.

value.question: Can a vision-language model save work by letting most picture pieces bypass the feed-forward block because that block barely changes them?
value.answer: Yes — this is the premise of Skip-Vision's Skip-FFN strategy: the authors observe that Feed-Forward Network computations on visual tokens induce only marginal feature updates, so they bypass FFN layers for redundant visual tokens [S1]. Combined with a selective KV-cache removal mechanism that prunes the skipped key-value pairs during decoding, this reportedly cuts training time by up to 35%, inference FLOPs by 75%, and latency by 45% while matching or exceeding existing methods' performance [S1].

value.question: ToDRE and DIVE both select visual tokens one at a time. What does each re-score candidates against?
value.answer: The provided sources describe only DIVE, not ToDRE. For DIVE, each iteration re-scores the remaining unselected candidates against the evolving prompt-conditioned residual state: after selecting the top-scoring token, the visual and query states are updated using the selected token's residual as feedback, so candidates are re-evaluated by their remaining (uncovered) visual residual energy weighted by alignment with the unresolved prompt [S1][S3]. This means candidates overlapping with already-retained evidence lose residual energy, while complementary, prompt-relevant candidates stay competitive [S1]. The sources contain no information about ToDRE's scoring criterion.

value.question: Once a few patches already describe an object, why is grabbing more patches of that same object wasteful?
value.answer: Because a token's value is not standalone but depends on its prompt-relevant residual state relative to the tokens already retained: once the selected tokens sufficiently characterize a salient object, keeping additional high-scoring patches from that same object region adds little new information [S2]. The remaining budget is better spent on previously uncovered image regions, secondary objects, or complementary contextual details, which is why static top-k pruning with fixed pre-computed scores is limited and DIVE instead re-scores candidates after each selection [S2]. Related work similarly notes that pruning should maintain spatial coverage across different objects and remove redundant (e.g., multi-view) tokens while retaining the most informative ones [S4].

value.question: Why can how much a region is looked at be a misleading guide to how much it actually changes the model's internal state?
value.answer: The sources don't address exactly this framing, but they report two related decouplings. In ControlMLLM, the relevancy between the model's output and pixels in the referring region keeps rising as the optimization steps T (or the step size α) grow, yet accuracy on the referred-object classification task drops — excessively large relevancy scores signal overfitting of the learnable latent variable rather than genuinely better grounding, which is why a relevancy around 0.18 tends to give the best performance [S1]. Conversely, in the operator-skipping analysis, the magnitude of visual-token updates (VUM) keeps growing in late layers while the answer-observable influence (AOI/AOE) of those updates declines, so raw update magnitude systematically overestimates the usefulness of late visual computation [S5]. Neither source directly measures attention-on-a-region against internal-state change, so that specific claim is not covered.

value.question: Why is keeping only the main subject of a photo not enough for every question people ask about it?
value.answer: Because a sizable minority of user queries are not about the main subject: across four VQA datasets, subject-related questions make up only about 73–80% of queries, leaving roughly 19–27% that are non-subject-oriented [S5]. These questions often hinge on subtle attributes outside the core subject region—e.g., reading sponsor logos on signage around a field rather than the athlete's jersey number, or checking whether a wine glass on the table contains liquid rather than the color of the bouquet [S5]. Consequently, pruning non-subject tokens risks discarding critical visual cues, so a mechanism that reuses or preserves their information is needed to keep performance robust [S5].

value.question: Can later layers keep reshaping picture features a lot while hardly affecting the final reply?
value.answer: The sources speak to the second half of that question but not the first. Several works indicate that deep-layer visual computation contributes little to the output: FastV reports that ~50% of image tokens can be dropped after layer 2 without sacrificing average performance across captioning, multiple-choice, OCR, video and fine-grained benchmarks, motivated by an observed "inefficient visual attention" phenomenon in later layers [S5]; ST³ finds token trimming hurts accuracy in shallow layers but is robust when applied to later layers [S3]; and a token-scheduling analysis notes that keeping non-subject visual tokens active late is inefficient because "little information is transferred in the later layers" [S1]. However, none of these sources measures how much the visual representations themselves are still being transformed in those late layers — CogVLM only remarks generally that visual features drift from the expected input distribution after multi-layer transformations in shallow-alignment designs [S2] — so the claim that features keep changing substantially while the reply stays the same is not directly supported here.

value.question: How can a multimodal model be pretrained faster by giving it fewer picture pieces early and more later?
value.answer: The sources describe DualSpeed, which speeds up MLLM training by feeding the model pruned visual token sequences rather than by a schedule of "fewer early, more later" [S3][S4]. Its fast-mode is the primary mode that plugs in existing visual token pruning methods to shorten the visual sequence, adding a learnable "mode isolator" soft prompt as a prefix so the LLM activates a distinct perception pattern for pruned inputs [S1][S3]; the auxiliary slow-mode trains on full visual sequences to preserve training-inference consistency and uses self-distillation from the sufficiently trained fast-mode (shared parameters, different inputs) [S3][S4]. The two modes switch randomly during training rather than in an early-to-late curriculum, and this yields 2.1\u00d7 speedup for LLaVA-1.5 and 4.0\u00d7 for LLaVA-NeXT while retaining over 99% performance [S3][S4]. The sources do not evaluate a staged schedule that increases token count over the course of training.

value.question: Why squeeze image features partway through the picture encoder instead of after it finishes?
value.answer: The provided sources don't address compressing or pooling features at an intermediate layer inside the vision encoder. They only describe compression applied to the encoder's final output \u2014 e.g., BLIP-2's Q-Former extracting a fixed number of query features from the frozen image encoder's features via cross-attention [S1], and AdaptVision projecting encoded patch features and then reducing local tokens to a quarter of their count with an additional linear layer [S3] \u2014 with no rationale given for doing this partway through the encoder instead.

value.question: Why do search systems that accept only one picture per query struggle with how-to guides?
value.answer: Because most existing multimodal retrievers permit only a single image in the query or document, they limit users' ability to clearly express their information needs and prevent the system from exploiting documents that contain multiple images and interleaved text-image content [S3]. How-to guides are exactly such documents: tutorials for everyday skills like furniture assembly or cooking recipes typically need multiple illustrations to describe sequential steps, and users may likewise need more than one photo to convey their problem or situation [S1][S3]. The paper notes that existing retrievers therefore struggle with text-image interleaved retrieval due to their single-image constraints [S1].

value.question: In models that fill in a masked reply step by step, does trimming picture input hurt more than in left-to-right generators?
value.answer: The sources do not contain a head-to-head comparison of how much accuracy is lost when pruning visual tokens in diffusion VLMs versus autoregressive VLMs, so this cannot be answered. They only note that visual token pruning was already proven effective for accelerating AVLM inference while it had not yet been explored for DVLMs [S3], and that within DVLMs, pruning visual tokens that are unimportant to the still-masked response tokens "does not significantly harm accuracy," whereas pruning guided by other token sets can remove tokens crucial to the masked tokens and cause accuracy drops [S1][S4]. Missing is any measurement of pruning-induced degradation in autoregressive models under comparable settings.

value.question: Can a mixture-of-experts vision-language model consult fewer specialists for picture pieces without losing much accuracy?
value.answer: Yes — FastMMoE, a training-free acceleration framework for MoE-based MLLMs, reduces expert activation for visual tokens to cut unnecessary expert computation, combined with routing-aware pruning that removes visual tokens with highly similar routing probability distributions [S2]. On large-scale MoE-MLLMs such as DeepSeek-VL2 and InternVL3.5, this reduces FLOPs by up to 55.0% while retaining about 95.5% of the original performance, outperforming dense-model pruning baselines like FastV and SparseVLM [S2]. The motivating insight is that in MoE models pruning a redundant visual token is equivalent to setting its expert activation count to zero, suggesting a sparser activation strategy for visual tokens generally [S1].

value.question: When the graphics card runs out of room mid-generation, how does the serving system decide whose work to set aside?
value.answer: vLLM uses first-come-first-serve scheduling, so when it runs out of GPU physical blocks for new KV cache it preempts the most recently arrived requests first, ensuring the earliest arrived requests are served first and preventing starvation [S2]. Because all blocks of a sequence are accessed together, it applies an all-or-nothing eviction policy (evict all or none of a sequence's blocks), and multiple sequences of one request (e.g., beam search candidates) are gang-scheduled as a sequence group that is always preempted or rescheduled together due to potential memory sharing [S2]. Evicted blocks can be recovered by swapping: their KV cache is copied to CPU memory managed by a CPU block allocator, and vLLM stops accepting new requests until all preempted sequences complete [S2].

value.question: Can models trained on land photos label sea creatures pixel by pixel without seeing any ocean images during training?
value.answer:
Yes, to a meaningful extent: the Earth2Ocean framework is a training-free open-vocabulary segmentation method that transfers terrestrial vision
text-language models (VLMs) to underwater domains without any additional underwater training, using a Geometric-guided Visual Mask Generator (GMG) that refines visual features via self-similarity geometric priors and a Category-visual Semantic Alignment (CSA) module that enhances text embeddings through MLLM reasoning and scene-aware templates [S4]. On the UOVSBench benchmark (AquaOV255 plus five other underwater datasets), this yields significant average performance improvement with efficient inference, producing accurate masks and category-pixel predictions without underwater training [S4][S2]. The capability is not unlimited, however: because it relies on terrestrial VLMs, segmenting extremely rare or visually ambiguous underwater species remains constrained, and the authors suggest pre-training underwater VLMs as future work [S2]. This is aided by the fact that language-supervised models like CLIP enable zero-shot transfer to downstream tasks without dataset-specific training [S3].

value.question: What end-to-end latency does HAWK achieve on an NVIDIA H100 GPU?
value.answer: The sources do not specify the GPU hardware used for HAWK's efficiency measurements, so I cannot confirm any H100-specific result. They report only that HAWK reduces end-to-end latency to 74.4% of the original [S1][S3], and on Qwen2.5-VL-7B/MME it cuts E2E latency from 20m 15s to 16m 10s (×1.25) at a 0.6 pruning ratio and to 15m 04s (×1.34) at 0.8 [S2], without stating the GPU model.

value.question: Can a system skip part of each network layer's work for image content instead of dropping whole layers or whole pieces of the picture?
value.answer: Yes. Skip-Vision applies a skip-FFN strategy in which many visual tokens are restricted to the attention layer and bypass the feed-forward network, reducing redundant computation while visual scaling is preserved [S1].
